hints: Look closely at the two curves in each graph. The solid line is with enzyme and the dashed line is without enzyme. Compare the height of the hump (peak) and check if S starts and P ends at the same level.
Remember what an enzyme actually does. It lowers the activation energy hump but it cannot change the starting energy of S or the final energy of P.
walkthrough:
**Spot what the axes mean**

Think of this like a hill you have to climb. S on the left is your starting energy, the top of the hump is the activation energy barrier, and P on the right is your finishing energy.

The barrier height is:
$$activation\ energy = peak\ energy - S\ energy$$

**Apply the enzyme rule**

An enzyme gives an easier route, so it lowers the hump. That means the solid line (with enzyme) must have a lower peak than the dashed line (without enzyme).

Crucially, an enzyme is a catalyst. It does not get used up and does not change S or P, so both curves must start at exactly the same S level and finish at exactly the same P level.

**Pick the matching graph**

Only graph C shows both rules. Same S start, same P finish, and the solid with-enzyme peak is lower than the dashed without-enzyme peak. That is the classic exothermic reaction profile with an enzyme.

options.A: Incorrect because the two curves finish at different P energy levels. An enzyme cannot change the energy of the product.
options.B: Incorrect because the solid with-enzyme peak is higher than the dashed peak. That would mean the enzyme increases activation energy, which is the opposite of its role.
options.C: Correct because S and P levels are identical for both curves, and the solid with-enzyme curve has the lower activation energy peak.
options.D: Incorrect because both the peak heights and the final P levels are different. The enzyme appears to raise the barrier and change product energy, which is impossible.
